data.title: Trump defends calling Putin a friend but won't say if he's a friend to the U.S.
data.description:
Trump defends calling Putin a friend but says he ‘can’t speak’ to whether he's a friend to the US

BILL BARROW and BEN FINLEY
Updated Fri, November 20, 2026 at 6:24 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his description of Vladimir Putin as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether the Russian president is a friend to the U.S.

Trump also insisted during a White House news conference that Putin wants peace with Ukraine, despite Russia's continued aggression after invading more than four years ago. Asked about the most recent attacks — hours after Putin met with Trump in China — Trump suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin share equal responsibility for the ongoing conflict.

"He'd love to end the war," the U.S. president said of his Russian counterpart. But, "you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other, Zelensky and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it."

Advertisement

During a wide-ranging news conference, Trump praised both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping after returning from China, where he participated in bilateral and trilateral meetings with his fellow heads of state.

Trump raised eyebrows on the trip with his warm welcome and repeated references to Putin as his "friend." He made no effort in the White House briefing room to walk back the comments. And he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the United States.

"I can't speak to America," Trump said, without expounding.

He shifted immediately to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin and repeated longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe that concluded that Russian agents sought to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election on Trump's behalf.

"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good."

"I've been dealing with Putin" since "the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax," as Trump calls the Department of Justice investigation. "It was a hoax made up by the Democrats" and "probably helped me win," Trump said.

Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is key to an eventual peace.

"You know, you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood on stage during Trump's news conference and made brief remarks, echoed the president's sentiments, pushing back against criticisms that Trump was embracing autocratic leaders as trusted allies.

"I want everybody to understand the relationships between heads of state are invaluable," said Rubio, who traveled with Trump to Asia. "It sets the tone for the entire relationship. It sets the tone for our trade negotiators. It sets the tone for our diplomats." __

Barrow reported from Atlanta.

data.title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on tech companies that build AI centers overseas
data.description:
US tech companies that build AI data centers in other countries will be penalized, Trump says

Associated Press
Updated Fri, November 20, 2026 at 5:45 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. tech companies will face "a tremendous tax" if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries, President Donald Trump said on Friday.

Trump did not provide details and said he hadn't yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterm elections.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centers," Trump said in a White House press briefing. "Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don't shut them off."

Advertisement

The Republican-led Senate on Thursday approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — perhaps the industry's biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.

Despite backing from Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic.

The tech industry says it has gotten the message. Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.

Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.

With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America's technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China's abilities to use U.S. chips to train its best artificial intelligence models.

data.title: 'We've got time': Trump now suggests Iran war will continue into 2027
data.description:
00:0004:42

Narrated by TIME AI.

President Donald Trump suggested he is putting off any major decisions on Iran until 2027, amid reports that he’s considering renewed major operations in the war that continues despite repeated promises that it’ll end soon.

Speaking to Reuters on whether new major strikes are possible—the U.S. has engaged in limited strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz—Trump, who was en route to Washington following his trip to China, said, “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.” He added: “We’ve got time.”

Trump made similar comments in other interviews. “We’ll see what happens after January 1st," the U.S. President told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, just before his summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He also told Axios in a phone call Thursday that he was “not rushing into any decision” on Iran.

The President initially promised that the war with Iran would only take weeks, but it has dragged on to nearly nine months, though major hostilities have subsided. Trump has previously said that the war would end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, but the impasse between Iran and the U.S. remained. And in the past weeks, he’s alternated between publicly threatening Tehran and holding off on authorizing new strikes at the request of American allies in the Gulf. 

Israel has reportedly tried to convince Trump of a new joint strike. The New York Times reported that the U.S. President is considering a new round of extensive military strikes on Iran, after Tel Aviv warned of Tehran’s “success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.” Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister whose premiership is in limbo, is reportedly pushing for a four- to seven-day airstrike campaign on Iran.

Advertisement

Axios reported, citing unnamed sources, that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios prepared by the U.S. military. Axios also reported that any U.S. campaign would involve Israel and could include strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, energy and other infrastructure, and Iranian military and civilian leaders. 

The U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress as the American public largely rebuked Trump and the Republican Party following their handling of the Iran war and the economic fallout it caused, could complicate decisionmaking. Before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump said that Iran was willing to strike a deal, but after the GOP’s stunning losses, which Iranian leaders celebrated, the Administration’s messaging pivoted to maintaining economic sanctions and the blockade on Iran.

Advertisement

Vice President J.D. Vance has blamed the war for the GOP’s election losses, but still appeared to defend the President’s foreign policy on Iran. The Vice President earlier said there was no difference between the President and members of his Administration on the war, but as Vance voiced his misgivings, Trump ordered the Vice President to shift his focus away from Iran diplomatic negotiations and toward domestic policies.

Trump has a small window to push through further military action against Iran before the newly elected Democrats take office in January. On Thursday, the GOP-led U.S. Senate rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war.

Trump addresses reported ‘dirty bomb’ threat 

In the interview with Fox News, Trump said he thinks people should not be alarmed by reports of a planned “dirty bomb” attack on Washington, D.C. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives like dynamite with radioactive material. 

Advertisement

“If it does happen, we wipe them out,” Trump said.

Trump acknowledged, however, that intelligence indicated Tehran is potentially interested in biological weapons. “Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear,” he said, referring to the damage that the U.S. has claimed it dealt to Iran’s nuclear facilities.

Iran’s foreign ministry refuted Trump’s recent statements. “The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar,” spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X.  “Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."

Baqaei then referred to how the U.S. justified its invasion of Iraq in 2003, alleging that the government of the late Saddam Hussein was developing weapons of mass destruction, which subsequent investigations found to be untrue. 

“We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations,” Baqaei said, “and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script.”

data.title: GOP leaders criticize members who are no-shows in Washington after losing re-election
data.description:
Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, talks with reporters in the US Capitol on Thursday, November 19.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

In one of Republicans’ final weeks in power, GOP leaders couldn’t convince enough of their members to come back to Washington to actually vote on their own bills — and Rep. Greg Murphy was furious.

Murphy, who just lost his eastern North Carolina seat in one of the biggest upsets of the midterms, unleashed on his GOP colleagues in a closed-door meeting Wednesday, urging leadership to cut off pay for any lawmakers who don’t show up, according to multiple people in the room.

“Look, I lost. I’m still here. I’m still here,” Murphy later told CNN about his frustrations at some of his colleagues’ delinquency. “If they aren’t here, they shouldn’t get paid.”

After their historic midterm rout, Republicans are increasingly exasperated at their otherwise-healthy GOP colleagues who are refusing to come back to Washington after their election defeats.

Speaker Mike Johnson and his GOP leadership team have been privately reprimanding those who chose not to come back, including one member who told the speaker they did not return because they were worried about a CNN report of the prospect of an Iranian “dirty bomb” plot in Washington. (Johnson, when learning of the reason for the member’s absence, reminded the member that their staff was in Washington working, according to a person familiar with the discussions.)

“Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” Johnson said Thursday. “We had 14 absences yesterday, so it’s not possible for us to advance a rule and advance our legislative agenda unless the members are here doing their job. … We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can’t do that unless people are present at work.”

It’s a glaring — and familiar — problem for Hill GOP leaders, who struggled all year trying to keep a record-small majority in line. And it comes as Republicans were already struggling with how to achieve as much of President Donald Trump’s agenda as possible before being pushed deep into the minority in January.

Republican leaders are under pressure to replenish Pentagon funding after months of war with Iran, but they don’t have the votes. They want to use their GOP trifecta to raise the debt limit to avoid a Democratic showdown with Trump next year. And they want to accomplish big legacy items, like permitting reform, before they’re forced to start over with Democrats in charge.

House Republicans believe the best way to accomplish Trump’s wants — particularly on the debt limit and Pentagon funding for the war — is by sidestepping Democrats altogether and doing a party-line bill. But any party-line bill is logistically challenging in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune has put a pause on his party’s push to take that route.

Now, Hill Republicans are increasingly worried they could squander their final days in power, with absences further complicating an already-difficult December puzzle. Some in GOP leadership privately fear that the only things Republicans will accomplish in December is punting government funding into the new year – maybe paired with an extension of the nation’s expired spy powers, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions.

They also worry about political theatre that could distract from the agenda, with GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a frequent leadership antagonist, forcing votes on the Epstein files and ending the Iran war.

Already, there’s some talk of sending the House home after passing a stopgap bill ahead of the December 11 funding deadline – and canceling the following weeks’ worth of scheduled votes – because Republicans won’t have the votes to do more, according to several of those people.

“There’s a possibility we can squander it if we don’t get our members back here,” senior GOP Rep. Mike Simpson said about the remaining days of Republican control. “What do we do to these guys that won’t come back?”

Rep. Jim Jordan, the incoming House GOP minority leader, is among the Republicans pushing to use that party-line process — known as reconciliation — to get Trump priorities done before the Democratic takeover.

“I’m in favor of getting as much done as we possibly can,” Jordan told CNN when asked about his preference for a GOP-only bill, adding he wants to see “all kinds of important things, like debt ceiling issue, like the defense issue.”

Asked whether that would include funding for Iran, Jordan added: “That’s certainly important.”

Thune, for his part, said Thursday that they likely won’t move ahead on a party-line bill until after Thanksgiving — when both chambers will have just three work weeks left. Many Republicans see it as a tacit acknowledgement that the party won’t get anything substantive done before handing over the gavels.

In the Senate, Republicans are squarely focused on confirming more Trump judges, landing a long-awaited permitting reform bill and finding a way to get money for the Pentagon.

Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota said he and others are still hoping Democrats will be willing to help pass some of that Pentagon funding — even as an emboldened Senate Democratic caucus makes clear that it won’t approve more money for the Iran war.

“They can vote against the military and tell everybody why they’re doing it,” Hoeven said of Democrats. “We’re trying to give them an opportunity to join us and do the right thing, which is vote support our military.”

If that doesn’t work, Hoeven acknowledged Republicans will need to try again on the party-line reconciliation push despite its difficulty.

But GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas was blunt about the prospects for that bill: “Everybody recognizes this is going to be a Herculean effort trying to get the House and the Senate to agree on the scope and the process.”

And Murphy, the North Carolina Republican chiding his colleagues for their absences, added this: “It’ll be hard if people don’t show up to their job.”

CNN’s Morgan Rimmer, Ted Barrett, Aileen Graef, Manu Raju and Logan Schiciano contributed to this report.

data.title: Democrats eye options to force an end to Iran war when they take control of Congress
data.description:
Politics

Democrats want to force Trump to end the Iran war when they take Congress. Can they?

By
Joe Walsh
Senior Editor, Politics
Joe Walsh is a senior editor for digital politics at CBS News. Joe previously covered breaking news for Forbes and local news in Boston.
Read Full Bio
Joe Walsh,
Caitlin Yilek
Politics Reporter
Caitlin Yilek is a politics reporter at CBSNews.com, based in Washington, D.C. She previously worked for the Washington Examiner and The Hill, and was a member of the 2022 Paul Miller Washington Reporting Fellowship with the National Press Foundation.
Read Full Bio
Caitlin Yilek

November 20, 2026 / 6:00 AM EST / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Washington — For months, Democrats have made ending the Iran war a core part of their pitch to midterm voters, promising that if they win control of Congress, they'll push President Trump to end an unpopular conflict that they blame for price increases.

Now, with Democrats set to take decisive majorities in the House and Senate next year, some members want to use the power of the purse to pressure the Trump administration to wind down the war, using must-pass bills as leverage. Exactly when — and how — they plan to act are less clear.

Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut told CBS News before the election that she would support "cutting off the funds for the Iran war." DeLauro is set to chair the powerful House Appropriations Committee, which has the ability to block funding. 

"If they want money, they have to get congressional approval," DeLauro said.

The first pressure point could arrive in a matter of weeks, before Democrats take control of Congress. Lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to extend funding for most federal agencies and prevent a government shutdown. Several Democrats have argued the party should block any stopgap bill that doesn't restrict funding for the Iran war. 

But some top House Democrats who will control key committees next year are backing away from that approach, warning it could lead to a shutdown.

DeLauro is part of government funding negotiations and favors a short-term extension until February if full-year appropriations measures are not passed by the deadline. She indicated that she is against using a continuing resolution as leverage. 

"I think that the American people would like to see us end the war," she told reporters Wednesday. "I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war." 

In a statement to CBS News on Thursday, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he would oppose a continuing resolution "if I believed shutting down government helped us actually achieve that."

"But I believe it would only shut down parts of government that Americans rely on," said Meeks, who is the incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The party's House and Senate leaders — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer — support ending the Iran war but have not specified what their approach will be, including whether they're open to attaching language to a stopgap funding bill.

Jeffries said Tuesday the House and Senate appropriations committees are in "active conversation" about how to fund the government. 

"I don't want to get out ahead of that process," he told reporters at a news conference. "What is clear is that the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran needs to end. It should end today."

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is challenging Schumer for majority leader, has argued the party should use the Dec. 11 deadline to force restrictions on the Iran war.

Van Hollen said in a statement last week that any funding deal "must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran." It was cosigned by Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and more moderate Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado.

Some Democrats also plan to offer amendments to any government funding deal to block war funding until the conflict is authorized by Congress, including Bennet, Duckworth, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Schumer-allied Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York.

Senate Democrats discussed how to proceed during a closed-door lunch meeting on Tuesday. Van Hollen told reporters they "had a very good discussion," but there was "no final decision."

Reps. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona and Ro Khanna of California said they would also vote against any funding package that "does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran." 

What could Democrats do next year?

After Democrats formally take control of the House and Senate in January, they could have several opportunities to attach Iran war-related language to must-pass legislation, in addition to voting on standalone bills and resolutions to restrict the war.

Lawmakers will likely need to extend government funding again, and they will need to raise the debt limit at some point next year. The appropriations process for the 2028 fiscal year and the annual National Defense Authorization Act are two other possible points of leverage.

Schumer told reporters earlier this month that "we are going to end the war," and said, "the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people."

Still, blocking the president from taking military action in Iran could be a challenging task.

"It is a complicated thing to force the president to stop using military force, and does require an alignment of political opportunity, savvy legislating, coordination that just is going to take time and political capital to implement," said Scott R. Anderson, a former State Department attorney and Brookings Institution senior fellow.

Mr. Trump has vowed to use his veto power liberally. Democrats would need support from several Senate Republicans and dozens of House Republicans to override his veto.

Beyond that, Mr. Trump and other presidents have claimed sweeping authority to direct the military. The president did not seek congressional authorization for the Iran war. Instead, he told lawmakers shortly after the war began that he "acted pursuant to my constitutional authority as Commander in Chief," in a notice issued under the War Powers Resolution, which requires the president to notify Congress of military hostilities within 48 hours.

That 1973 law also limits hostilities to 60 days — with an extra 30-day grace period to withdraw troops — unless lawmakers pass an authorization for use of military force, and it allows Congress to pass resolutions directing the president to terminate hostilities before then.

House and Senate Democrats have used that law to vote to terminate hostilities several times this year, drawing support from some moderate or anti-interventionist Republicans. One war powers resolution cleared both chambers in June. But the Trump administration has brushed off those votes, arguing the War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional. On Thursday, the Senate blocked another House-passed resolution, losing Republican support for reining in Mr. Trump on Iran. 

Jeffries said Tuesday that House Democrats are discussing whether to force more votes on war powers resolutions this year. 

"It's something that's under discussion right now, and we'll take a look at vehicles that we have available to us," he said. "But it certainly is the case that early on in the new Congress, we're going to aggressively move to end the reckless Republican war of choice in Iran." 

Later in the day, during an interview at the Atlantic Summit in Washington, Jeffries indicated that Democrats would vote next year on a resolution "that has the force of the law."

The resolution that cleared the House and Senate in June was passed under a procedure that did not require the president's signature.

Jeffries said the goal is to send a war powers resolution to Mr. Trump's desk, essentially daring him to veto it. The war remains deeply unpopular with Americans. 

"There's nothing more powerful than putting that bill on the president's desk," Jeffries said.

Meeks told CBS News that starting in January, "I will introduce a War Powers Resolution, support legislation that cuts off funding for this war, and require the administration to take diplomacy seriously by sending real diplomats, not the president's golf buddy and son in law."

Other Democrats have backed using funding bills as leverage. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said in one recent interview that if the Trump administration doesn't follow already-passed war powers resolutions, "our only choice is to use the appropriations process to forbid funding for war operations, unless the president gets the legally required authorization by Congress."

Asked about Democrats' plans, a White House official told CBS News: "As President Trump and Secretary Rubio stated, our economic pressure campaign is devastating Iran to such an extent that the President does not have any need to conduct major combat operations."

"The Democrats continue to prove that have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to baselessly obstruct the President's agenda," the official said.

What could restrictions on the Iran war look like?

There is some history of Congress constraining the president's ability to make war. In 1973, the House and Senate overwhelmingly passed legislation blocking the government from using funds for hostilities in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. Then-President Richard Nixon signed it into law.

Anderson told CBS News that if lawmakers want to force an end to the Iran war, they could pass legislation that either prohibits hostilities with Iran outright or bars the president from using federal funds to pay for the war, or both.

"You need some sort of affirmative bar to block the president from acting," he said. "Even then, there's kind of a question of, 'Does the president listen? How enforceable is it?'"

Another open question: What specific military actions Democrats might try to ban.

The U.S. has not conducted large-scale offensive operations against Iran in recent months, but the conflict has remained at a simmer. The two countries have exchanged occasional strikes — typically after the U.S. military alleges imminent threats from Iran — and the U.S. has enforced a blockade on Iranian ports and escorted oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Anderson says Congress could try to bar the Trump administration from resuming offensive bombings, and the blockade on Iran could also be restricted. Defensive operations are likely to be exempted, though the bill would need to be worded carefully.

In the past, Anderson notes, presidents have argued the Constitution inherently gives them the power to carry out operations to defend U.S. nationals, regardless of any legislative complications — an argument President Gerald Ford used to evacuate Saigon and order some other operations around the tail end of the Vietnam War.

"If you do an absolute funding cutoff, what do you do when you have U.S. vessels traversing the Strait of Hormuz and they do get shot at by Iranians, or American sailors get captured?" he said.

Democrats have yet to publicly lay out a plan for how they plan to counter the administration if it defies Congress on ending the war. If Democrats believe the administration isn't complying with its obligations, the House or Senate could sue, but the outcome could be hard to predict.

Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, has argued that impeaching Mr. Trump over the war should be an option. 

"How are we going to stop him? What law are we going to pass when he chooses not to obey the law?" Smith said in an interview with CNN last month, prior to the election. 

Smith told The New Republic earlier this month that even if Democrats forbid any funding for the war, "the legal language and the loopholes — the ways that Trump can sort of jump out of it — those will all continue to be challenges."

"We are headed into uncharted territory here," Smith said. 

Anderson said he believes Democrats are serious about passing restrictions on the Iran war, but it could take multiple attempts and plenty of "political fighting and legal maneuvering."

"People do need to be patient," Anderson said. "There is this expectation that Democrats won and the Iran war will end tomorrow. That is not what is going to happen."

  • Iran war powers measure again falls short in Senate

  • Iran may be working on biological weapons, Trump says

  • U.S. launches strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in Strait of Hormuz

data.title: Russian missiles hit Poland as Moscow unleashes a massive attack on Ukraine
data.description:
Russia pummels Ukraine, missile hits Poland, after Putin threat

Célia LEBUR and Victoria LUKOVENKO
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 12:31 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Moscow pounded Ukraine with massive strikes Friday, with Kyiv saying at least six people were killed in the capital, and neighbouring Poland reporting two Russian missiles likely landed in the south-east corner of the NATO country, accusing Moscow of a "provocation."

Hours earlier, Russia's Vladimir Putin vowed a "painful" response to Kyiv's strikes on Moscow's Crimea bridge after holding a summit with China's Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky called the night-time strikes one of Moscow's largest of the entire war, denouncing Russian "terror."

Advertisement

Zelensky -- who met with allies in Berlin Thursday -- said Putin's attempts to "redraw the world" with Xi and Trump had been a "failure."

In China, Putin said he "shared responsibility" for global peace with Xi and Trump and issued a "declaration toward peace" that made no mention of Moscow's almost five-year invasion of Ukraine.

AFP journalists saw people hunkering in Kyiv's metro stations -- which double as overnight air-raid shelters -- sleeping on yoga mats, camping chairs and in pop-up tents.

Kateryna Liubychenko, 32, had taken her toddler down to try to get some sleep through the bombardment.

"It's painful to have to stop our child from living," she told AFP.

Another two people were killed in Lviv, power was knocked out in swathes of the country and in Kyiv, three vital transport bridges were hit, officials said.

Explosions rang out through the night as Ukrainian officials reported more than 80 missiles and 400 drones were fired.

"Kyiv: The death toll from last night's Russian attack has risen to six. Another 15 people were injured," Ukraine's emergency service said amid the rescue operation.

Three bridges that cross the Dnipro river were also hit, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, threatening yet more disruption to daily life in the city.

France requested a UN Security Council meeting over the strikes, saying "Russia will have to answer for its actions there."

- Poland decries 'provocation' -

In neighbouring Poland, authorities said one missile was confirmed to have landed in the eastern village of Nowy Lipowiec, with another missile and a jet-powered drone suspected to have hit two other locations.

Warsaw said no-one was hurt.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the weapons flying into Poland were deliberate.

"The provocation may have been linked with the fact that there are (military) exercises taking place on the territory of Poland," Tusk told a televised press conference in Warsaw.

Thousands of European troops are taking part in military exercises in southeastern Poland.

"Nobody can say that this was an innocent coincidence," Tusk said, adding he had informed NATO "straight away."

Tusk said that NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte would be in Warsaw on Saturday and that he would inform him of the incident.

Poland is one of five countries Europe picked to represent it at future US-led talks on Ukraine.

- Bridge retaliation -

Russia, which has refused a ceasefire, has increased its strikes as temperatures dip in Ukraine, with many fearing this winter could be the worst of the war yet.

Kyiv's state energy operator reported "significant damage" to the country's energy infrastructure that had "seriously impacted the operation of the power grid".

The Black Sea port city of Odesa was in a "critical" situation with a "widespread power outage", it said -- adding blackouts were also recorded in Kyiv and ten other regions.

Russia's military on Friday confirmed it had launched a "massive" attack with missiles and drones, saying they targeted military-industrial sites and transport infrastructure in several regions, including bridges in Kyiv.

The UN has reported rising civilian casualties this year as Russia intensifies its long-range strikes.

UNICEF on Friday said at least 114 children had been killed and 1,030 wounded in the first 10 months of 2026 -- "a higher number of verified child casualties than in any of the past three years."

"That is on average of more than three children killed or injured every single day," the organisation said, warning of an "alarming escalation in violence affecting children in Ukraine."

US-led talks on ending the fighting have so far shown little signs of progress, with Moscow having stuck to its hardline demands.

Putin has said a deal to end the war in Ukraine must be part of a wider agreement on European security.

Speaking in China on Thursday, he said any form of Ukraine-Europe military cooperation as part of that deal would be a "problem".

data.description:

Trump’s National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross fired amid widespread tech outages

Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies will step into the role as acting national cyber director after Cairncross's departure

By Brittany Miller Fox News

Nationwide tech, banking and flight outages spark social media panic

New York Post columnist Rikki Schlott, The Federalist reporter Brianna Lyman and political commentator Joe Sweeny join 'Fox & Friends' to discuss viral social media panic over recent tech outages.

NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles!

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out after President Donald Trump backed his firing over concerns he lacked the cybersecurity credentials for the job, Fox News has confirmed.

Kirsten A. Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, will step into the position in an acting capacity. 

Davies, who was Senate-confirmed, will join Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, White House technology advisor Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the administration's national security and cyber leadership team.

An administration official separately told Fox News that Cairncross did not want to serve another two years in the role. Cairncross took office Aug. 4, 2025, after Senate confirmation, and the exact date of his departure remains unclear.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired from his job after a series of major tech outages. (Godofredo A. Vasquez/AFP via Getty Images)

Senior administration officials welcomed Davies' appointment on X.

"Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity," Rubio wrote.

Clayton praised her background, writing, "With nearly two decades of leadership experience in the technology space, Kirsten Davies will be a strong asset for the Trump administration in her new position with the Office of the National Cyber Director. It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape."

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth wrote, "The Department congratulates Kirsten Davies on her new role as the National Cyber Director. Throughout her tenure at DOW, she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape."

US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT

Davies thanked Trump, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Hegseth in her own post on X, calling the moment a critical juncture for U.S. technology.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future," Davies wrote. "I am honored to continue to serve."

The leadership shakeup follows a nearly weeklong stretch of technical disruptions that hit air travel, major banks, Microsoft services, Apple, Marriott, the National Weather Service and internal systems at the National Security Agency. 

A Nov. 13 Federal Aviation Administration outage triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight cancellations after contractor work on air traffic control wiring overloaded the system.

Administration officials have pushed back against speculation that hackers or foreign adversaries were behind the disruptions. Rubio said Tuesday that officials found "zero evidence" tying the incidents together or to malicious actors, while Clayton said the outages appeared linked to routine software patches and system upgrades rather than a coordinated cyberattack.

DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

Department of War Chief Information Officer Kirsten A. Davies testifies during a Senate Armed Services subcommittee hearing on cybersecurity on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on March 24, 2026. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The Office of the National Cyber Director and Cairncross did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

data.title: Russia fires 100 missiles at Ukraine hours after Trump talks peace with Putin
data.description:
The western city of Lviv hit by Russian attacks overnight

The western city of Lviv hit by Russian attacks overnight
0:41

Link Copied!
Kyiv — 

Moscow launched a deadly missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight into Friday, just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin met his US and Chinese counterparts for historic trilateral talks in which the three powers billed themselves as a force for peace in the world.

Trump spoke to European leaders after the call, reportedly describing Putin as “tired” and ready for peace. But Kyiv said Russia fired at least 100 missiles overnight - an unusually large number even amid Russia’s frequent aerial assaults.

Eight people have been killed and at least 28 injured during the massive attack which has so far lasted more than eight hours, according to Ukrainian authorities.

Some 400 drones, including 120 jet-powered drones which are essentially compact cruise missiles, were also part of the attack.

The Polish government said on Friday that fighter jets were scrambled and Patriot air defense systems activated early on Friday after Poland’s airspace was violated during the attack, with “objects” flying in and falling inside the country’s territory.

Smoke billows above Kyiv skyline as explosions heard in Russian missile attack
0:30 • Source: CNN
Smoke billows above Kyiv skyline as explosions heard in Russian missile attack
0:30

The deadly assault came hours after Putin left China following a day of meetings in Shenzhen with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

The talks failed to produce any breakthrough on Moscow’s more than four-year war in Ukraine, and appeared to be used by Putin as an opportunity to repeat his maximalist demands and false narratives about the conflict in front of a global audience.

The Russian leader hailed the summit with Xi and Trump as historic and told reporters the discussions took place in a “relaxed and very intimate atmosphere.”

In his opening remarks, Putin said Russia, China and the US have “shared interests” in settling the Ukraine war.

People enter a Kyiv metro station to shelter overnight following warnings of possible Russian air attacks early on November 20, 2026.

No official declaration or a readout were released after the talks, but Trump did speak afterwards to the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine’s key allies which was convening with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Berlin.

According to a senior European official with knowledge of the call’s contents, the president’s main message was that “Putin is tired, wants to end this, ready for a deal.”

The official said Trump’s suggestion was “to reach out and grasp at the opportunity.”

He said the Europeans were “constructive in response but want proof.”

Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who was part of the call, said that Trump sounded “fairly optimistic.”

“Although I have to say (his words) were received very cautiously in the room, when it comes to Putin’s and Moscow’s intentions regarding peace talks.”

“But I don’t hide the fact that I’ve heard this very often from President Trump. His belief in Putin’s goodwill seems unshakable, even though so far there are no facts to support it, he said, adding that it “would be good, if it really turned out that Russia was genuinely ready to engage in peace talks.”

Kushner said Trump had conveyed “a very strong message to both of them [Xi and Putin] on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”

Strikes target key bridges

Russia’s defense ministry said in a post to Telegram it launched a “massive strike using high-precision weapons from land, sea, and air,” as well as drones, targeting Ukrainian military and energy facilities, port infrastructure in the Odesa region, and transport infrastructure in Kyiv.

But Kyiv said Moscow’s targets included a hospital in Kharkiv and residential buildings in the Dnipropetrovsk, Lviv, Vinnytsia, Sumy, and Chernihiv regions.

Three of Kyiv’s bridges were damaged in the overnight strikes, according to mayor Vitaly Klitschko, halting transport links connecting the two sides of the capital.

“All emergency services have done and will continue to do everything possible to mitigate the consequences of the attack as quickly as possible,” Klitschko said, adding that people should avoid traveling if possible.

The deadly attack came after Putin vowed revenge for Ukraine’s recent attacks on prized project, the strategic multibillion-dollar bridge linking Russia with the occupied Crimea.

“There will be no negotiations,” he said. “I believe our response, as I have just said, will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge.”

The attacks have also knocked down power in several regions across Ukraine, just as temperatures are beginning to drop to bellow zero.

Several districts in Kyiv were without power due to the attack, according to energy company DTEK. Emergency power outages have also been implemented in the Lviv, Zakarpattia, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, according to Ukrenergo, the country’s state-owned electricity operator, which called the situation in the power grid “extremely critical.”

CNN’s Nick Paton Walsh and Victoria Butenko contributed reporting.

data.title: Senate passes bipartisan bill to make data centers pay for their energy use
data.description:
Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs

MATTHEW DALY
Updated Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:04 AM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Climate COP31 Data Centers

1 of 6
FILE - An Amazon data center is under construction in New Florence, Mo., Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Jeff Roberson, File) (AP Photo/Jeff Roberson)

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

Advertisement

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE" in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, "lowering Energy Costs for American Families," Trump wrote.

Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

"Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.," said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill "a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America" and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.

Democrats push for amendments

A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

"Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn't tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that," Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for "purely political purposes."

The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of "a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.

"I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet," Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project's possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

"In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build," said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. "Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years" as they await approval by the federal government.

"Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box," driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber's energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families," Lee said.

Co-sponsor calls bill 'the floor, not the ceiling' for legislative action on climate

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is "the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations," adding that he hopes "to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities" over the next two years.

But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation's bodies of water, land and wildlife.

"Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process" to debate and amend the bill, she said. "Don't sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it's currently drafted, is not the answer."

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. "Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation," he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.

"A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill," Granholm wrote in a social media post. "But it would still need this president's signature."

Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would "irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home." He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California's environment.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.
